% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval,
%          w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval

\subsection{Composability with Fine-Tuned Models}
\label{sec:composability-ft}

The cross-model validation in \S\ref{sec:cross-model} establishes that
OntoCoDec generalizes across model families in the zero-shot regime.
A complementary question is whether the same constraints remain useful
after task-specific fine-tuning, where the model has been trained to
emit ontology-conformant outputs and one might expect violations to
disappear on their own.
We test this by LoRA fine-tuning both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B on
SciERC and then evaluating each fine-tuned model with and without the
two-layer constraints, yielding a 2$\times$2 design per model family.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.4pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll rr rr@{}}
\toprule
& & & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{Viol.~(\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){4-5} \cmidrule(l){6-7}
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Train} & \textbf{Decode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & CF
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{4}{*}{Qwen3-8B}
  & Zero-shot & U   & 15.37 & 0.08 & 8.23 & 31.01 \\
  & Zero-shot & S1  & \textbf{0.93}  & 9.90 & 8.36 & 30.98 \\
  & LoRA      & U   &  1.95 & 0    & 43.86 & 67.05 \\
  & LoRA      & S1  & \textbf{0.00}  & 1.18 & 43.77 & 67.05 \\
\midrule
\multirow{4}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B}
  & Zero-shot & U   & 13.34 & 0.24 & 2.68 & 23.56 \\
  & Zero-shot & S1  & \textbf{0.08} & 6.56 & 2.54 & 23.49 \\
  & LoRA      & U   &  1.11 & 0    & 45.45 & 67.76 \\
  & LoRA      & S1  & \textbf{0.09} & 0.46 & 45.47 & 67.76 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}%
\caption{Composability with fine-tuning on SciERC (551 documents).
U: unconstrained; S1: full two-layer decoding.
LoRA $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, all-linear targets, 3 epochs, effective batch 16.
F1 $\times$100. RV and ET are 0\,\% in every constrained row and are
omitted for space.}
\label{tab:composability}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Fine-tuning does not eliminate ontology violations.}
LoRA fine-tuning lifts relation F1 from 8.23 to 43.86 (Qwen) and from
2.68 to 45.45 (Llama)---a 35--43\,pp gain that brings both models well
above the zero-shot regime.
% w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval: R-F1=0.4386; w5_llama_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval: R-F1=0.4545
Yet residual domain/range violations persist at 1.95\,\% (Qwen) and
1.11\,\% (Llama), and per-relation analysis shows tight-constraint
relations remain problematic: Evaluate-for retains 13.1\,\% DR for the
fine-tuned Qwen model despite achieving zero on six of the other seven
relations.
% w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval.notes: Evaluate-for DR=13.13%
This pattern matches the tightness-driven mechanism of
\S\ref{sec:method}: relations whose valid type pairs cover a small
fraction of $|\mathcal{T}|^2$ resist coverage even at the data
distribution level, because the long tail of contexts is unlikely to
be exercised during fine-tuning.

\paragraph{Constraints compose with fine-tuning at no F1 cost.}
Applying full S1 decoding on top of the fine-tuned models eliminates
residual DR almost entirely (Qwen 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0.00\%, Llama
1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\%) while relation F1 changes by less than 0.1\,pp
($-$0.09\,pp Qwen, $+$0.02\,pp Llama) and entity F1 is identical to
the fine-tuned unconstrained baseline in both cases.
% w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval: DR=0, R-F1=0.4377, E-F1=0.6705 (vs U: 0.4386, 0.6705)
% w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval: DR=0.0009, R-F1=0.4547, E-F1=0.6776 (vs U: 0.4545, 0.6776)
The fine-tuned model has already moved its output distribution away
from gross violations, so the constraint mask only intervenes on the
small residual mass; the cost of that intervention is negligible.
The CF rate at the fine-tuned regime is also markedly lower than at
zero-shot (1.18\,\% Qwen, 0.46\,\% Llama vs.\ 9.90\,\% and 6.56\,\%),
consistent with our analysis that CF reflects semantic ambiguity in
borderline assignments: fine-tuned models commit to more confident
type predictions, leaving fewer borderline cases for the per-relation
mask to flip.

\paragraph{Implication.}
Fine-tuning and decoding-time enforcement are complementary, not
substitutable.
Fine-tuning is the primary lever for extraction \emph{quality} (F1),
while constrained decoding is the primary lever for ontology
\emph{compliance} at the long tail.
A practitioner who fine-tunes for F1 still needs constraint
enforcement to deliver per-instance type validity, because the
relations with tightest constraints---those most important to enforce
in safety-critical settings---are precisely the ones fine-tuning is
least likely to cover from data alone.

\section{Extended Discussion}\label{app:discussion}

%%% Paragraph 1: Low F1 Practical Significance %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%), phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%),
%          phase0_scierc_unconstrained (DR=15.37%), phase2_docred_unconstrained (DR=18.46%)

\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% on both SciERC and DocRED reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve approximately 49--53\% relation F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
When applied to fine-tuned models that reach competitive F1 levels, the same constraints remain necessary---Phase~0 analysis confirms that even well-prompted models exhibit non-trivial violation rates (15.37\% DR on SciERC, 18.46\% on DocRED).
% exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_docred_unconstrained
In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting isolates its effect from confounds introduced by task-specific fine-tuning.

%%% Paragraph 4: Decoding-Time vs. Post-Hoc Enforcement %%%
% exp_ids: posthoc_filtering_baseline, phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%),
%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%, ET=0%)

\paragraph{Decoding-Time vs.\ Post-Hoc Enforcement.}
Post-hoc filtering---generating triples without constraints, then removing schema-violating predictions---yields higher precision and consequently higher F1 than OntoCoDec on both datasets (SciERC 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED 9.61 vs.\ 8.23).
% posthoc: SciERC F1=8.63, DocRED F1=9.61; OntoCoDec: SciERC R-F1=8.36, DocRED R-F1=8.23
However, this precision gain comes at substantial cost.
On DocRED, post-hoc filtering discards 48.1\% of all predicted triples, including 127 true positives (11.2\% of correct predictions), reducing recall from 9.46\% to 8.40\%.
% posthoc_docred: rejection=48.1%, tp_lost=127/1137, R: 9.46→8.40
Entity type violations remain unresolved (ET\,=\,2.47\% vs.\ OntoCoDec's 0\%), as filtering targets only domain/range and vocabulary violations.
% posthoc_docred: ET_residual=2.47%; phase2_docred_full_s1: ET=0%
OntoCoDec's decoding-time approach avoids this information loss by guiding generation toward compliant outputs rather than discarding non-compliant ones, preserving both recall and entity type validity.
The two strategies are complementary: post-hoc filtering can serve as an additional safety net for residual violations that decoding-time enforcement does not fully resolve.

%%% CF--DR Re-routing analytical finding (W1 pilot) %%%
\paragraph{CF--DR Re-routing: Why the Current Design Is Near-Optimal.}
A natural question is whether the elevated CF rate under full S1 can be
reduced by triggering grammar-first fallback whenever the semantic layer
would assign an entity a type inconsistent with a previously registered
assignment for the same entity.
We piloted this variant on SciERC with Qwen3-8B and observed that CF drops
sharply from 9.90\,\% to 0.04\,\% ($-$9.86\,pp), but DR \emph{rises} from
0.93\,\% to 14.78\,\% ($+$13.85\,pp), nearly matching the unconstrained baseline.
% w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot: DR=0.1478, CF=0.0004; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093, CF=0.099
The combined violation budget $(\text{DR}+\text{CF})$ therefore grows from
10.83\,\% to 14.82\,\%, a net increase of 3.99\,pp; relation F1 is essentially
unchanged ($-$0.13\,pp, 8.36\,$\to$\,8.23), and entity F1 is identical to baseline.
% R-F1 8.36→8.23 (-0.13pp), E-F1 30.98 unchanged
The fallback mechanism fires on 36.6\,\% of mask calls overall, with a
CF-registry-specific trigger rate of 4.5\,\% (17{,}024 mask calls; 6{,}237
fallback events).
% w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot: grammar_first_fallback_rate=0.3664, cf_registry_fallback_rate=0.0448
These numbers reveal a fundamental tension: the two violation types
draw from the same pool of constrained tokens.
Triggering fallback to satisfy cross-entity coherence releases the
domain/range guarantee for the token in question, re-routing the
violation rather than eliminating it.

\paragraph{Schema ambiguity dominates residual CF.}
We further decomposed the 245~CF-affected entities by conflict pattern and
found that 60 (24.5\,\%) involve \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$\textsc{Other\-Sci\-en\-tific\-Term},
and 63.3\,\% in aggregate trace to entity types that appear in the
domain/range of multiple relations with cross-cutting type intersections
(e.g., \textsc{Method}$\cap$\textsc{Task}, \textsc{Material}$\cap$\textsc{Generic}).
% w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot.notes: dominant pattern Generic↔OtherScientificTerm 60/245
These conflicts reflect genuine schema-level ambiguity---multiple
relation-specific type assignments are simultaneously ontologically valid---rather than enforcement-side failures.
Per-relation independent enforcement is thus the appropriate locus of
control: globalizing the registry would either re-route violations
(as shown above) or require offline disambiguation outside the
generation loop.
We conclude that the current two-layer design occupies a near-Pareto-optimal
position on the (DR, CF, F1) frontier: any attempt to reduce CF through
local intervention shifts cost to DR with no net violation reduction.
Genuine CF resolution requires global entity-level type consensus,
which we identify as future work (\S~Limitations).
